title: SLO-aware quant economics notebook
body:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory sheet + reasoning for SLO-aware quantization recommendations. This is a working notebook: aggregator of simple formulas, scenario table, and operational guidance for picking INT8/FP8/4-bit variants depending on latency SLO, sequence-length distribution, and quality budget.

High-level problem:
- Customers care about 3 dimensions: unit cost ($/1M tokens), P95 latency (ms) and quality delta (task-specific metric e.g., EM/ROUGE/accuracy).
- Quantization impacts compute throughput (=> cost), kernel behavior (=> latency distribution and warmup jitter), and numerical fidelity (=> quality delta).
- Need pragmatic rule-of-thumb and a micro-model that teams can plug in per-customer workload (seq length histogram, batch size, qps).

Key assumptions (editable):
- base_gpu_cost_per_hour = $3.60 (example; G4-like equivalent) => base_gpu_cost_per_second = 0.001
- tokens_per_gpu_second (FP32 baseline) = 2500 (depends on model/seq)
- quant_speedup_factors: INT8 = 1.8x, FP8 = 1.4x, 4bit = 2.6x (these are measured medians; tweak per model)
- quality_delta tolerance = acceptable degradation relative to baseline (e.g., 0.5% absolute or 1% relative depending on metric)
- batching_effect = effective increase in tokens/sec due to batching; depends on latency SLO and request parallelism

Formulas (plain):
- gpu_cost_per_second = base_gpu_cost_per_hour / 3600
- effective_tokens_per_second = tokens_per_gpu_second * quant_speedup_factors * batching_effect
- cost_per_1M_tokens = (1_000_000 / effective_tokens_per_second) * gpu_cost_per_second
- p95_latency_estimate_ms = baseline_p95_ms / quant_speedup_factors * latency_penalty_factor
  where latency_penalty_factor captures kernel jitter/warmup and smaller-batch inefficiencies (>=1)
- quality_delta_pct = measured_metric_baseline - measured_metric_quant

Quick worked example (numbers illustrative):
- base_gpu_cost_per_hour = $3.60 => gpu_cost_per_second = $0.001
- tokens_per_gpu_second_FP32_baseline = 2500
- batching_effect = 1.2 (typical for short bursts and light batching)
- For INT8 speedup 1.8x: effective_tps = 2500 * 1.8 * 1.2 = 5400 TPS
- cost_per_1M_tokens = (1_000_000 / 5400) * 0.001 = $0.185 per 1M tokens
- If FP8 speedup 1.4x -> effective_tps = 4200 -> cost_per_1M = $0.238
- 4bit speedup 2.6x -> effective_tps = 7800 -> cost_per_1M = $0.128

But caution: these cost estimates ignore failure modes: INT8 might cause cache-eviction pattern changes that raise p95 by 20% in some kernels for long-seq cases. FP8 may have smaller quality deltas on long-context tasks but lower speedup on quant-friendly kernels. 4bit can be fastest but quality regressions are sometimes concentrated on rare tokens leading to visible hallucinations in evaluative slices.

Operational SLO-aware heuristic (first-draft rules):
- If target_p95_ms <= 200ms and median_seq_length <= 256 and quality_budget_pct >= 0.7%: prefer INT8.
- If target_p95_ms in (200, 600] and workload is batchable (99th percentile batch_size >= 4) prefer FP8 for better quality stability.
- If cost pressure is extreme (>2x cheaper needed) and we can accept manual quality gating (eval sets + rerank), consider 4bit for non-customer-facing backend tasks (embeddings, bulk summarization).
- For mixed workloads: route: interactive requests -> INT8 (fast), background/bulk -> 4bit (cheap). Use automatic fallback if quality regression detected on a per-prompt eval set.

SLO routing policy sketch (pseudocode):
- if request.latency_budget_ms < 250:
    try INT8 primary variant
    if quality_delta > threshold for that tenant (computed on recent evals) -> fallback to FP8
  else if request.can_batch:
    prefer FP8 or FP32 if quality regression seen
  else if cost_multiplier_target < 0.6:
    consider 4bit but gate via rerank-of-top-k on a higher-fidelity variant

Open questions / TODOs:
- Replace rough speedup_factors with measured per-model kernel benchmarks (Ablation: seq length 64/256/1024/4096).
- Add term for memory-bound cases (where KV cache growth reduces effective speedup).
- Model cost impact of autoscaling granularity (per-GPU vs per-pod) — small bursts can dramatically increase per-token cost if autoscaler steps are coarse.
- Build a small experiement pipeline: take 3 reference workloads (chat, code-completion, long-doc-summarization), run across FP32/FP16/FP8/INT8/4bit, capture TPS, p95, and several quality metrics.

Notes for solutions/eng: practical checks when enabling quant variant in Dedicated/Private: 
- Ensure kernel fallback path exists for operand shapes that blow up quant kernels (rare long sequence edge cases).
- Add an on-host canary that runs a small eval suite after variant promotion.
- Tag telemetry: quant_variant, seq_length_bucket, batch_size, kernel_warmup_count, quality_score_delta — easy to correlate when alerts fire.

Recommended immediate next steps (short runway):
1) Run median-bench for 3 popular models and populate speedup_factors and p95_penalty by seq bucket. (owner: Marco).
2) Wire a small SLO-routing prototype in the simulator to validate heuristic under synthetic traffic patterns (owner: Leah).
3) Draft a short customer FAQ about when we recommend INT8 vs FP8 vs 4bit and what signals will trigger an automatic fallback/pin (owner: Aisha).

Appendix: compact calculator cells (text):
- A1: base_gpu_cost_per_hour = 3.60
- A2: gpu_cost_per_second = A1 / 3600
- B1: tokens_per_gpu_second = 2500
- C1: quant_speedup (user input)
- D1: batching_effect (user input)
- E1: eff_tps = B1 * C1 * D1
- F1: cost_per_1M = (1_000_000 / E1) * A2

End of notebook. This is intentionally an editable working doc — keep iteration in Drive.
conclusion: Draft ready for benching; goal is to ship a short, one-page customer recommendation and an internal SLO-routing prototype in the next 3 sprints.
